Reproduced at the National Archives at Seattle 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Indian Agency, Nespelem, Wash. Jan. 26, 1920 Mr. C. V. Peel, Special Agent in Charge, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Peel; Louise Michel, the mother of Henry Michel, has called at this office and shown me a letter dated January 13, from Peter Moses to his father, Joe Moses, alleging that Henry Michel is sick and wants to go home. Mrs. Michel has also shown me a letter from Henry dated January 21, addressed to his sister, Susanne Michel, stating that he is just about to enter the hospital. He states, "I don't think Morgan will let me go home if I do ask him." Mrs. Michel is naturally concerned as to Henry, and I have assured her that we have received no reports here that he is sick, and that I had no reason to believe that there was anything serious ailing him. I wish that you would have Henry write to his mother assuring her as to his condition and I believe that a letter from you to her would quiet her anxiety. I regret the evident inclination on Peter's part to incite dissatisfaction at the school. Very truly yours, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent COLD 1-26 to 1-29 RS:AJ Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Feb. 2, 1920 Mrs. Louise Michel c/o Colville Indian Agency Nespelem, Washington Dear Madam: I have received a request to write you in regard to your boy, Henry. It seems that he has been writing you that he is sick and wants to come home. I have to advise that, so far as I can ascertain, he had one or two little colds during the month of January and was sent to the school hospital for treatment, as is done in all cases when a pupil has the least kind of illness. You probably know that we maintain a hospital in connection with our school here and it is just a few rods from the several dormitories and when a pupil becomes the least bit ill, we send him, or her, to the hospital for treatment. Henry has not been seriously ill at any time. If he had been, we would have notified you, but we think it unnecessary to notify parents when their child happens to have a little cold or cough. As far as I can learn, Henry is getting along nicely in school and is learning something every day which is bound to benefit him throughout his life time. Should he go home now, he probably would never enter school again and would no doubt go thru life and will be sorry that he did not stay in school as long as he possibly could. I would be very glad to see him finish his term here this year and if this school is permanently closed in June to enter the Indian school at Chemawa, Oregon, next fall. Trusting that this will ease your conscience as to your son's welfare, I am Yours very truly, Special Agent in Charge. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., June 12, 1919 My dear Mr. Michell: I have been informed that you are objecting to your son's accompanying our Band on its summer trip. I am sure your objections are based on a misunderstanding of the purpose of this trip and the uncertainty as to whether your son will be properly cared for during this trip. Mr. Fred W. Freeman is an Indian employee who has been detailed to accompany the Band for the sole purpose of seeing that your son, and the other boys, receive careful attention and care. Mr. Freeman's son, Freddy, who is about ten years old, is a member of the Band and will accompany the Band, and I assure you that Mr. Freeman will take just as good care of your son as he will of his own. The boys will be looked after as carefully as if they were at home and will not be allowed to wander about unless accompanied by Mr. Freeman. They will be under his eyes and in his care every moment of the time they are away from this school, until they return and, when they do return, they will be given permission to visit home before school, so that their parents will see that they have been well taken care of and will hear from them all about the wonderful things they have seen and heard during their trip. If the boys were to pay for this trip, it would cost them not less than $1,000.00 to make it. They will visit sixty-eight cities and will play before the President of the United States. It is a wonderful opportunity and I feel sure you will not be so selfish as to rob your boy of the chance to go with his fellow school-mates of the Band. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. EHH:MG Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Nov. 2, 1918. Mr. Mike Mechell, Omak, Washington. Dear Mr. Mechell: I am returning herewith money orders #22950 and 22951 for $7.00 each, purchased at Omak, Wash., sent to Henry and Suzanne Mechell, would advise that the Cushman School does not close for vacation until next June 1919, when your children will be allowed to return home for the vacation. Suzanne has been ill with the grippe, but is now well again, and has left the hospital. If you desire this money placed to the credit of your children until they are ready to return home for the vacation next June, you may send it back to me, and I will keep it on deposit here for them. Yours very truly, Superintendent Omah. Wash., Oct. 28, 1918. Dear Henry's, I am now sending you a few dollars for the expense to come back for vacation when they let you go from school. I am waiting for you here at Omak Washington. Let me know soon as possible. We are all well and happy. Yours Truly, Henry & Susan Machell, Cushman Trade School, Tacoma, Wash. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington April 8, 1919. Mr. Fred C. Morgan Nespelem, Washington. Dear Mr. Morgan: Replying to your letter of April 2, 1919, regarding the return of Henry Michell to help his father plow. Henry has on deposit here the sum of $10.00. Leave of absence for two weeks will be given him at your request. Please have him return promptly at the expiration of his two weeks as he should not really be out of school a single day. Very truly yours, Superintendent MHH:T enc 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash., April 2, 1919. Mr. E. H. Hammond, Supt., Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Hammond: Mike Michel, father of Henry Michel, requests that you permit Henry to come home for three weeks to assist in plowing on the home place. Mike has no one else to assist in this necessary work and if Henry can be spared I recommend that you grant him the leave of absence requested. If he is to be allowed to come home he should come at once as spring plowing has already begun in this neighborhood. If additional money is required, kindly advise me and sufficient amount will be transferred. Very truly yours, Fred C. The law provides: "That no part of this appropriation, or any other appropriation provided for herein except appropriations made pursuant to treaties, shall be used to educate children of less than one-fourth Indian blood whose parents are citizens of the United States and of the State wherein they live and where there are adequate free-school facilities provided and the facilities of the Indian schools are needed for pupils of more than one-fourth Indian blood." EXTRACTS FROM SCHOOL RULES. If the facilities of a school are not needed as provided in the above paragraph, children showing any Indian blood, whose parents live on an Indian reservation, and who if debarred from Government schools could not obtain an education, may be enrolled in the day and boarding schools of their reservation; the children, however, may not be transferred to nonreservation schools without special permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Before enrolling a pupil superintendents must satisfy themselves whether he has left any other school without permission and whether he has been expelled for cause from any other school. A pupil who has been expelled for cause from any Indian school may be reenrolled in any Indian school only with permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Attention is invited to Circulars Nos. 1039 and 1044, which must be observed. "The Secretary of the Interior may in his discretion withhold rations, clothing, and other annuities from Indian parents or guardians who refuse or neglect to send or keep their children of proper school age in some school during a reasonable portion of each year."
